title: Free-text Rationale Generation under Readability Level Control
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be prompted to generate free-text rationales at different readability levels, and whether those readability instructions change both the content and perceived quality of the explanations. The authors frame the work as a perturbation test of natural language explanations: if rationales can be steered by readability prompts, they may behave more like general text generation than like fixed internal explanations of model decisions.

The approach uses instruction prompting to request explanations targeted at four readability levels (college, high school, middle school, and sixth grade), mapped to Flesch Reading Ease ranges. The study evaluates generated rationales with automatic readability metrics, reference-free TIGERScore, BERTScore, and human annotations. Experiments are run on four NLP tasks with explanatory annotations: fact-checking (HealthFC), hate speech classification (HateXplain), hate speech detection (CAD), and natural language inference (SpanEx), using four open-weight LLMs (Mistral-0.2, Mixtral-0.1, OpenChat-3.5, and Llama-3). Human validation is conducted on HateXplain with five annotators who rated readability, coherence, informativeness, and label agreement.

The main findings are that LLMs do respond to readability instructions, but the resulting text complexity only partially matches the intended levels. Rationales tend to cluster around medium complexity, and both metric-based and human judgments often favor high-school-level explanations. The authors conclude that rationale generation is sensitive to prompting and shares characteristics with controllable text generation, but current readability control is imperfect and evaluation remains challenging because of hallucination, metric limitations, and weak alignment between metric scores and human perceptions.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical NLP study, but it is not a K-12 intervention trial. The evidence is observational/benchmark-based with human judgment components rather than a controlled educational design, so it fits a lower-certainty qualitative/correlational tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest, indirect impact: readability prompting can alter explanation style and perceived usefulness, but it does not test student learning gains or classroom outcomes. The relevance to education is secondary and the measured effects are not tied to K-12 achievement or behavior outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based free-text rationale generation under prompted readability-level control, using instruction prompting to make explanations target sixth-grade, middle-school, high-school, or college readers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether readability-controlled LLM rationales preserve task accuracy across fact-checking, hate speech detection, and NLI. Task accuracy varies substantially by model and dataset (e.g., OpenChat-3.5 reaches 82.1% on SpanEx, while performance is much lower on HateXplain and HealthFC), but readability prompting itself does not systematically improve or degrade accuracy; the main finding is that task predictions remain broadly consistent while rationale text complexity changes.
finding.measure: Task accuracy on classification/fact-checking benchmarks (HateXplain, CAD, SpanEx, HealthFC)
finding.study_size: multiple datasets; test sizes reported as n=1,924 (HateXplain), n=5,307 (CAD), n=3,865 (SpanEx), n=750 (HealthFC)

finding.finding_summary: The core substantive outcome is explanation quality/readability as a form of clarity and communicative usefulness. Human annotators generally found the rationales satisfactory across all readability levels, but agreement on the intended readability levels was low (Krippendorff’s α = 3.67%, Fleiss’ κ = 13.92%), and annotators only recognized the prompted readability level correctly 23.7% of the time. High-school-level rationales were most commonly perceived and favored, indicating that the intervention changes expression but only imperfectly achieves the targeted audience adaptation.
finding.measure: Human ratings of readability, coherence, informativeness, and accuracy; readability metrics (FRE, GFI, CLI)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can be steered to generate rationale text at different readability levels via prompting, which may help automate explanation tailoring without additional fine-tuning. However, the generated complexity only loosely matches the target levels, so the efficiency gain is in controllability rather than precise compliance.
finding.measure: Readability metrics on generated rationales and model-following of instructed output format
finding.study_size: multiple model-dataset runs; exact total n not reported
